whyThisMatters: Permits, dry-dock invoices, tracking-system alerts, and charter instructions are how Operations keeps the fleet moving — and exactly what attackers copy, because a request that looks like routine fleet paperwork rarely gets a second look. Today you will build the habit of checking the sender's exact domain and confirming any change to a payment, permit, or instruction through the process you already follow, not the email alone.
rememberThis: A vendor invoice, a permit request, or a system alert that looks routine is not proof by itself. STOP before you approve a bank-detail change, skip a safety sign-off, or act on an urgent alert — VERIFY through your own known channel or console, then REPORT anything that pushed you to skip that step.

discussionPrompts: Ask what the team's actual permit-to-work process is — is there ever a real exception for "just this once", and who would actually be allowed to grant it?
For the dry-dock invoice card, ask how the team would verify a changed bank detail without using any contact information supplied in the email itself.
For the fleet-tracking alert, ask what a genuine urgent alert from your own monitoring tool actually looks like — does it ever ask for a password through a link?
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often miss the safety sign-off bypass and PSC detention cards, because an unreachable supervisor or an official-sounding notice both feel like a reason to act fast rather than check. The habit to build is the same one every card points to: verify through your own known channel — a callback, your PSC liaison, your port agent — before you skip a step or pay anything.

items.title: Real vs Fake Permit-to-Work Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake email comes from a different domain (synergymarine-hse.net vs synergymarinegroup.com). It asks Ops to skip a required safety sign-off "just this once", and promises to "backfill the paperwork later" — never a legitimate safety process.
items.whyItsSuspicious: An unreachable supervisor plus a request to skip a safety sign-off is the same social-engineering pattern as a fake-boss payment scam, just aimed at a safety process instead of money. A real permit-to-work process has no "just this once" exception, no matter who is claimed to be asking.

items.title: Real vs Fake Dry-Dock Invoice Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake email comes from a different domain (fleet-drydockservices.net vs fleetdrydock-services.com). It asks to change payment details based on the email alone, with an artificial deadline tied to the vessel's departure from the yard.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Real dry-dock and vendor payments only change through a verified update to the vendor master file, never a one-off email instruction. A schedule-based deadline like "before the vessel departs" is a classic pressure tactic used to make you skip that check.

items.title: Real vs Fake Fleet Tracking Alert
items.whatIsWrong: The fake alert comes from a different domain (synergy-fleettrack.net vs synergymarinegroup.com). It invents an impossible 5-minute deadline tied to a scary claim of lost vessel-position data, with a direct login link instead of pointing to the dashboard you already use.
items.whyItsSuspicious: A genuine fleet-tracking alert gives you time and points you to the dashboard you already have bookmarked — it never asks for your username and password through a link, and losing tracking data is not fixed by "re-logging in" through an email link anyway. The scary operational claim is designed to make you skip that check.

items.title: Real vs Fake Port State Control Notice
items.whatIsWrong: The fake notice comes from an external, generic-sounding domain (port-stateauthority.net) rather than your own internal PSC liaison or a documented official channel. It asks for a direct fee payment via email, which real Port State Control processes never do, with a detention threat attached.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Real Port State Control deficiencies and any associated fees go through your own company's agent and documented official channels, verified against the actual inspection report — never a payment request that arrives cold by email with a detention threat. Verify any such notice with your own PSC liaison and port agent before any payment is considered.

items.title: Real vs Fake Charter Party Amendment Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake email comes from a different domain (bluewave-charter-ops.net vs bluewave-charterers.com). It asks for a major operational change — redirecting the vessel — based on the email alone, with no signed addendum, citing an invented commercial emergency.
items.whyItsSuspicious: A genuine charter-party amendment as significant as redirecting a vessel always comes with a signed addendum through the agreed charter-desk process — never a same-email instruction to act immediately. This is the same fake-authority pressure pattern as any other Business Email Compromise attempt, just aimed at operational instructions instead of a payment.
